q_822206bdbfef.explanation: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity inside an AWS Region.

optionNotes.A: CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches content at edge locations; it is a service, not an environment made of data centers.
optionNotes.B: An Availability Zone consists of one or more discrete data centers within a Region, which is exactly what the question describes.
optionNotes.C: A VPC is a logically isolated virtual network that you define; it is not a physical group of data centers.
optionNotes.D: Outposts is AWS infrastructure installed at a customer site, not an environment defined as one or more AWS data centers.

q_aa55b1e4a4d7.explanation: AWS does not charge for data transferred in from the internet, so inbound transfer of 2 TB is the free option. The other listed transfers are generally charged.

optionNotes.A: Data transferred in to AWS from the internet is not charged, so this is the no-cost transfer.
optionNotes.B: Data transferred out from AWS to the internet is charged per GB (after any free tier allowance).
optionNotes.C: Data transferred between AWS Regions is charged, because the traffic leaves the source Region.
optionNotes.D: Data processed by a NAT gateway is charged per GB, so it is not free.

q_a8cbe4ca36bb.explanation: AWS Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises while staying connected to an AWS Region, which is a hybrid deployment model.

optionNotes.A: An on-premises model runs entirely in the customer's own facilities without using AWS as part of the deployment; Outposts connects on-premises resources to AWS.
optionNotes.B: Serverless describes services such as Lambda where you do not manage servers; it does not describe on-premises AWS hardware.
optionNotes.C: A cloud-native model runs fully in the cloud, while Outposts places AWS hardware at the customer's site.
optionNotes.D: Hybrid combines on-premises infrastructure with the AWS Cloud, which is what Outposts provides.

q_6d65a98f156c.explanation: Deploying to multiple AWS Regions places the application in several geographic areas so it can serve users worldwide.

optionNotes.A: A multi-Region architecture runs the application in several Regions around the world, meeting the global deployment requirement.
optionNotes.B: A single-Region deployment keeps everything in one geographic area, so it is not a global deployment.
optionNotes.C: Multi-AZ improves availability inside one Region but does not spread the application across the globe.
optionNotes.D: Single-AZ runs in one data center group in one Region, which is the opposite of a global deployment.

q_945e2036e8dc.explanation: AWS Outposts puts AWS infrastructure in the company's own facility, so data stays on premises with low latency to local resources while still using AWS services and APIs.

optionNotes.A: Local Zones are AWS-operated sites near large cities; the data would sit in AWS facilities, not on the company's premises.
optionNotes.B: Availability Zones are AWS data centers within a Region, so data would not remain on the company's premises.
optionNotes.C: Outposts installs AWS infrastructure on premises, keeping data local and giving low latency to nearby systems.
optionNotes.D: Wavelength Zones are embedded in telecommunications providers' networks for mobile low latency, not in the company's own facility.

q_239a160f0c63.explanation: Global reach is the cloud benefit of deploying applications to users worldwide using AWS Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations.

optionNotes.A: Economy of scale means lower prices from AWS's large volume of usage; it does not describe worldwide deployment.
optionNotes.B: Global reach lets a company deploy to users anywhere through Regions, AZs, and edge locations.
optionNotes.C: Agility is the ability to provision and experiment quickly, not geographic coverage.
optionNotes.D: High availability concerns staying operational during failures; the scenario is about reaching users around the world.

q_849e34b5cd58.explanation: Availability Zones in the same Region are separate locations in one geographic area with independent power and networking, so placing EC2 instances in multiple AZs meets all the requirements.

optionNotes.A: Edge locations are used by services like CloudFront for caching and do not host EC2 instances for independent power and networking.
optionNotes.B: Multiple AZs in one Region are in the same geographic area but have independent power grids and networking.
optionNotes.C: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service and has no locations for placing EC2 instances.
optionNotes.D: AWS Artifact provides compliance reports and has no locations for placing EC2 instances.

q_be38c294a4ef.explanation: AWS Outposts brings AWS infrastructure and services into the company's own site, giving low-latency access to on-premises systems and keeping supported data in place for residency needs.

optionNotes.A: Wavelength embeds AWS compute in telecom providers' networks for ultra-low latency to mobile 5G devices; it does not place AWS infrastructure at the company's own site for on-premises systems.
optionNotes.B: Transit Gateway connects VPCs and on-premises networks; it does not run AWS infrastructure on site or address data residency.
optionNotes.C: Ground Station is a service for communicating with satellites and is unrelated to on-premises latency or data residency.
optionNotes.D: Outposts runs AWS infrastructure on premises, giving low latency to local systems and keeping supported data on site.

q_58ea2edfaca4.explanation: There are more edge locations than Regions, and there are more Availability Zones than Regions because each Region contains multiple AZs. So more edge locations than Regions and more AZs than Regions are the correct statements.

optionNotes.A: Each Region has multiple Availability Zones, so there are fewer Regions than AZs, not more.
optionNotes.B: AWS has far more edge locations than Regions, so this is true.
optionNotes.C: An edge location is a separate type of site used for caching and delivery; it is not an Availability Zone.
optionNotes.D: Edge locations greatly outnumber Regions, so there are not more Regions than edge locations.
optionNotes.E: Every Region contains multiple Availability Zones, so total AZs exceed the number of Regions.

q_9cfa8622081d.explanation: The AWS global footprint lets a company choose the specific Region, and therefore the geographic area, where an application is hosted to meet regulations.

optionNotes.A: Scalability is about adjusting capacity to demand and does not control where an application is located.
optionNotes.B: The global footprint of Regions in many geographic areas lets the company host the application where regulations require.
optionNotes.C: Availability is about keeping the application running and does not decide which geographic area hosts it.
optionNotes.D: Performance relates to speed and latency, not to meeting a geographic regulatory requirement.

q_ebf12e3ef27c.explanation: AWS Regions and Availability Zones are the core building blocks of the AWS global infrastructure (alongside edge locations). The other options are services that run on top of it.

optionNotes.A: Availability Zones are the data center groups inside Regions and form part of the global infrastructure.
optionNotes.B: ElastiCache is a managed in-memory caching service that runs on the infrastructure; it is not part of it.
optionNotes.C: Regions are the geographic areas that make up the global infrastructure.
optionNotes.D: Amazon S3 is a storage service that runs on the global infrastructure, not a part of it.
optionNotes.E: A VPC is a virtual network you create within a Region; it is a service, not part of the physical global infrastructure.

q_a82dd006dfb8.explanation: AWS Outposts runs AWS services on hardware in the company's own facility, so applications controlling factory equipment communicate locally with the least latency.

optionNotes.A: Outposts runs AWS compute on site next to the factory equipment, giving the lowest latency.
optionNotes.B: EC2 normally runs in an AWS Region, so traffic to the factory must cross the network to AWS and back.
optionNotes.C: Lambda runs in an AWS Region and adds network distance from the factory equipment.
optionNotes.D: Fargate is a serverless container engine that runs in a Region, so it is not located next to the factory.

q_5cfba44f46ca.explanation: AWS Outposts extends AWS infrastructure, services, APIs, and tools to data centers, co-location spaces, or on-premises facilities for a hybrid architecture.

optionNotes.A: Snowmobile is a truck-sized device for moving exabytes of data to AWS; it does not extend AWS services on premises.
optionNotes.B: Local Zones are AWS-operated extensions near large cities; they are not installed in the customer's own data center.
optionNotes.C: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure, services, APIs, and tools to the customer's own facilities, enabling hybrid architectures.
optionNotes.D: Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers and does not extend AWS infrastructure to customer sites.

q_eab56f93dd2b.explanation: AWS Outposts runs workloads on premises for regulatory reasons while using the same AWS APIs, tools, and services as the cloud.

optionNotes.A: Dedicated Hosts give a physical EC2 server for licensing or compliance but do not extend AWS APIs to on-premises workloads.
optionNotes.B: Outposts installs AWS infrastructure on premises and uses the same APIs as in the cloud, so both sets of workloads are managed consistently.
optionNotes.C: Availability Zones are AWS data centers, so workloads would not run on the company's premises.
optionNotes.D: Wavelength places compute in telecom networks for mobile low latency, not on the company's premises.

q_875e8ec9600a.explanation: The AWS global infrastructure of Regions, Availability Zones, and edge locations lets a company run applications and deliver content close to users around the world, lowering latency.

optionNotes.A: Regions and edge locations around the world let the company place applications and content near users to reduce latency.
optionNotes.B: Pay-as-you-go pricing is a billing model and does not affect latency.
optionNotes.C: Managed services reduce operational work but do not bring applications closer to users.
optionNotes.D: Economy of scale lowers prices and does not improve latency for global users.

q_e7bee2939470.explanation: AWS Outposts lets the company run AWS services in the cloud while keeping part of the workload on its own premises for compliance.

optionNotes.A: AWS Config records and evaluates resource configurations; it does not run workloads on premises.
optionNotes.B: Outposts brings AWS infrastructure into the company's own data center, supporting a hybrid split between cloud and on-site workloads.
optionNotes.C: Lightsail is a simple managed service for virtual servers and small apps in AWS; it does not place workloads on site.
optionNotes.D: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service and has nothing to do with hosting workloads on premises.

auth-global-infrastructure-01.explanation: An Availability Zone is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity, located inside a Region.

optionNotes.A: This reverses the hierarchy: a Region contains multiple Availability Zones, not the other way around.
optionNotes.B: A site that caches content for CloudFront is an edge location, not an Availability Zone.
optionNotes.C: This is the definition of an Availability Zone: one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity in a Region.
optionNotes.D: AWS hardware installed at a customer's own data center describes AWS Outposts, not an Availability Zone.

auth-global-infrastructure-02.explanation: Legal and regulatory requirements come first, because a Region outside the EU cannot be used however cheap or feature-rich it is. Price, services, and latency are weighed only among compliant Regions.

optionNotes.A: Price matters, but it is considered only after the Region satisfies the data residency rule.
optionNotes.B: Newer services are a secondary factor and cannot justify storing EU patient records outside the EU.
optionNotes.C: Developer location is not a primary factor and is irrelevant to the legal residency requirement.
optionNotes.D: The regulation requires data to stay in the EU, so compliance with data residency is the first filter for choosing a Region.

auth-global-infrastructure-03.explanation: With no compliance limits, a company should weigh latency to end users and pricing in each Region (along with service availability). Prices for the same service differ between Regions.

optionNotes.A: Latency to end users affects application performance and is a standard factor when choosing a Region.
optionNotes.B: The number of IAM users does not differ by Region, because IAM is a global service.
optionNotes.C: Prices for the same service vary between Regions, so cost is a standard selection factor.
optionNotes.D: A Support plan applies to the whole account and does not change from Region to Region.
optionNotes.E: Existing S3 data size is not a Region selection factor for a new application, and S3 buckets can be created in any chosen Region.

auth-global-infrastructure-04.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that caches content such as videos at edge locations near viewers and can use an S3 bucket as its origin, which speeds up loading for distant students.

optionNotes.A: Global Accelerator improves the network path to endpoints using static IPs but does not cache video content at the edge.
optionNotes.B: CloudFront caches the videos at edge locations close to students, reducing load times from an S3 origin in one Region.
optionNotes.C: Outposts runs AWS infrastructure in a customer's facility and does not cache content for users on other continents.
optionNotes.D: Route 53 is a DNS service that routes users to endpoints; it does not cache or deliver video content.

auth-global-infrastructure-05.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator provides static anycast IP addresses and routes TCP or UDP traffic over the AWS global network to the nearest healthy endpoint in one or more Regions.

optionNotes.A: CloudFront is aimed at caching and delivering web content, not at providing static IP entry points for UDP game traffic.
optionNotes.B: Local Zones extend a Region to a metro area for low latency but do not provide static anycast IPs that route to healthy endpoints across Regions.
optionNotes.C: Global Accelerator gives fixed static IPs and sends TCP or UDP traffic over the AWS global network to healthy endpoints in several Regions.
optionNotes.D: Wavelength places compute inside telecom provider networks for mobile users and does not provide static IPs routing to multiple Regions.

auth-global-infrastructure-06.explanation: Local Zones place compute, storage, and other services close to large population centers for low-latency workloads such as media production, without the customer hosting hardware.

optionNotes.A: An AWS-operated extension of a Region placed near a metro area, giving single-digit millisecond latency with no hardware to host.
optionNotes.B: Outposts gives low latency but needs AWS hardware installed at the customer's own site, which the company wants to avoid.
optionNotes.C: CloudFront is a content delivery network that caches content near viewers; it does not run the editing application's compute.
optionNotes.D: A distant Region adds network distance, so it cannot give single-digit millisecond latency to editors in the city.

auth-global-infrastructure-07.explanation: AWS Wavelength deploys AWS compute and storage inside telecommunications providers' data centers at the edge of their networks, giving low latency to 5G mobile devices.

optionNotes.A: Local Zones sit near large cities but are not inside the mobile carriers' networks.
optionNotes.B: Outposts installs AWS hardware at a customer's own site and is not embedded in telecom provider networks.
optionNotes.C: Direct Connect is a dedicated network connection to AWS and does not host compute at the telecom edge.
optionNotes.D: Wavelength embeds AWS compute and storage in telecom providers' networks so 5G devices reach the backend with ultra-low latency.

auth-global-infrastructure-08.explanation: Running instances in at least two Availability Zones and using a load balancer to spread traffic across them keeps the application available if one AZ fails. Options that stay in one AZ fail together with it.

optionNotes.A: A larger instance type adds capacity but the instances still sit in the same failed Availability Zone.
optionNotes.B: Instances in at least two Availability Zones mean the application keeps running if one AZ fails.
optionNotes.C: More instances in the same AZ all fail together when that AZ fails.
optionNotes.D: A load balancer across multiple AZs sends traffic only to healthy instances in the remaining AZs.
optionNotes.E: An Auto Scaling group confined to the current AZ cannot launch instances elsewhere when that AZ fails.

auth-global-infrastructure-09.explanation: For regional services, data created in a Region stays there unless the customer copies or replicates it elsewhere, which supports data residency; AWS's exceptions are limited to what is needed to provide the services the customer chose or to comply with law. Regions have multiple AZs, and services are not equally available in every Region.

optionNotes.A: Public Regions are built with at least three Availability Zones, so the number is not fixed at two.
optionNotes.B: Regional services keep data in the chosen Region unless the customer explicitly copies or replicates it elsewhere (AWS moves content only as needed to provide the services the customer chose or to comply with law).
optionNotes.C: Service availability differs between Regions, and new services often launch in some Regions first.
optionNotes.D: An edge location is a separate type of site for content delivery and is not a type of Region.

auth-global-infrastructure-10.explanation: Deploying in multiple Regions supports disaster recovery if an entire Region is unavailable and gives lower latency to users on different continents.

optionNotes.A: Extra Regions do not add Availability Zones to an existing Region; each Region has its own set.
optionNotes.B: Components spread across Regions have higher latency between them, so this is a reason to keep them in one Region.
optionNotes.C: A second Region lets the workload recover from a disaster that makes an entire Region unavailable.
optionNotes.D: A multi-Region design needs more data replication between locations, not less.
optionNotes.E: Placing the workload in Regions near users on different continents lowers latency for each group.
